sm: Casey Luskin argues that the objection that intelligent design is not science fails for several reasons. He says philosophers have no agreed definition of science, that design meets rigorous methodological definitions because it uses the methods of historical sciences, and that it meets practical criteria through a research program with hundreds of peer-reviewed papers. He also says critics apply arbitrary requirements such as methodological naturalism, and he invokes Stephen Meyer's principle that any definition disqualifying design would also disqualify evolution. He then defines intelligent design as a theory that uses historical science methods to infer that many features of nature are best explained by an intelligent cause, because they show information and complexity that in our experience only come from a mind. He describes it first as a theory of design detection, citing William Dembski on information and Meyer on specified complexity, especially codes and languages.

Luskin explains specified complexity, also called complex specified information. Information is complex if it is unlikely, but unlikely alone does not signal design, as with everyone's seat in a room or a poker hand. It must also match an independent pattern, which he calls specification. He illustrates this with a string of zeros and ones that turns out to be binary code spelling a Richard Dawkins quote about biology looking designed, and with a visitor named Yodel who sees an oddly shaped mountain as natural but recognizes Mount Rushmore as designed. He then describes how design theorists build detection criteria by studying designed objects and human designers. Those criteria include specified information, irreducible complexity, blueprints, purpose or function, reuse of parts across designs, and coordination of parts. He says finding these in nature is a positive way to detect design.
